title: Why Is There Something?
objective: After this level you can explain Leibniz's question of why there is something rather than nothing and his answer from sufficient reason.
summary: Leibniz’s principle of sufficient reason leads him to ask why there is something rather than nothing and to answer with a necessary being; Russell replies the universe is just there.

cards.headline: Why is there anything at all?
cards.body: Not why there are stars, or cats, or you. Why is there something rather than nothing? Leibniz thought it was the first question anyone may fairly ask.

cards.headline: Nothing without a reason
cards.body: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646-1716) was the first to name the principle of sufficient reason and treat it as a major principle of philosophy. In Principles of Nature and Grace (1714) he puts it plainly: nothing comes about without a sufficient reason. For any truth, someone who understood enough could say why it is so rather than otherwise.

cards.headline: The first question
cards.body: Given that principle, Leibniz says, the first question we can fairly ask is: why is there something rather than nothing? After all, he adds, “nothing is simpler and easier than something.” An empty world would need no explaining. A full one does. Look around: you are surrounded by the harder option.

cards.headline: Leibniz’s answer
cards.body: The reason can’t be found inside the series of changing things. Each motion comes from an earlier one, and going further back just repeats the question “Why?”. So the reason must lie outside the series, in something that exists necessarily and carries the reason for its existence within itself. That ultimate reason, Leibniz says, is what we call God.

cards.headline: Maybe it’s just there
cards.body: Critics answer that the demand itself may be the mistake. In a 1948 radio debate with Frederick Copleston, Bertrand Russell said the universe is “just there, and that’s all”: a brute fact, needing no explanation. Much earlier, in Hume’s Dialogues, the character Cleanthes argued that if you explained each of twenty particles, it would be unreasonable to then ask for the cause of the whole twenty.

cards.headline: Why Is There Something?: the big picture
learned: Principle of sufficient reason: nothing without a reason
Leibniz: a necessary being outside the series
Russell: the universe is just there

questions.prompt: What principle does Leibniz build his big question on?

options.label: Nothing is more real than the eternal Forms
Everything that exists can be perceived
Nothing can ever be known for certain
Nothing comes about without a sufficient reason

questions.explanation: The principle of sufficient reason: nothing comes about without a reason why it is so rather than otherwise.

questions.prompt: Why does Leibniz think the reason for the universe must lie outside the series of changing things?

options.label: Because tracing each motion to an earlier one never stops the “Why?”
Because the series of changing things is too short to hold a reason
Because Russell showed the universe is a brute fact
options.rationale: Russell was his critic, centuries later.

options.label: Because an empty world would need more explaining than a full one
options.rationale: He says the reverse: nothing is simpler.

questions.explanation: Every motion comes from an earlier one, so the question “Why?” always remains; only a necessary being outside the series could stop it.

questions.prompt: Leibniz demands a reason why for everything. What did Aristotle give in Level 5 when asked why a statue exists?

options.label: No answer: he called it a brute fact
options.rationale: That’s Russell’s move about the universe.

options.label: The Form of Statue, apart from the bronze

questions.explanation: Aristotle’s four causes are four kinds of answer to a why-question, and a full explanation can use all four.
